title: The latency your users feel is not the one on your dashboard
angle: Serving teams graph total request duration for a streaming endpoint, then tune against a number that mostly measures how long the answers happened to be. The split into three latencies is cheap, and it is what makes every other decision attributable.
thesis: For a streaming LLM endpoint, total request duration is the wrong primary metric: it is dominated by output length, which is a property of the answer rather than of the service, and tuning against it hides the four serving failures that users actually report.

sections.heading: A streaming endpoint has three latencies
sections.claim: Time to first token, inter-token latency and total duration are three different measurements with three different causes, and only the first two are properties of the service.
sections.evidence: The decomposition, what each one is felt as by the user, and the rule that a duration percentile over mixed traffic measures the traffic mix.

sections.heading: Five symptoms that arrive as one complaint
sections.claim: The single report 'it is slow' covers five distinct failures, each with a different check.
sections.evidence: Diagnostic table: user-visible symptom, likely cause, and the specific metric split that separates it from the others.

sections.heading: Where the queue actually is
sections.claim: Continuous batching moved the admission limit from a batch-size constant to key-value cache memory, and the usual capacity signals did not follow.
sections.evidence: Why high GPU utilisation is not fullness, why reserving cache by requested maximum output length wastes the limiting resource, and why an aggregate percentile hides an interactive class sharing a node.

sections.heading: The decision rule
sections.claim: Attributing time to first token into queue wait and prefill compute determines which fix applies.
sections.evidence: Four-branch rule with the fix for each branch, and a floor below which the search should stop.

sections.heading: Order of operations
sections.claim: The order of the fixes matters more than the fixes, because the cheap reversible ones are also the ones that make the expensive ones measurable.
sections.evidence: Numbered sequence from splitting the metric to changing the model, with the reason each step precedes the next.

sections.heading: The trap nobody checks
sections.claim: A load test whose output-length distribution does not match production invalidates every capacity conclusion drawn from it.
sections.evidence: The concrete check: output tokens per request, production against load test, on the same axes; plus the log-only version for teams with no harness.

sections.heading: Where this stops applying
sections.claim: The advice is bounded by who owns the serving stack and by the model's own floor.
sections.evidence: Three named limits: hosted APIs, a model too slow for the interaction, and non-streaming clients for which only total duration matters.

gaps: No first-token latency or inter-token latency figures from a deployment he has run. Every number in the piece is either arithmetic or a public property of the serving stack; if he wants a measured example, the 'five symptoms' section is where it would go.

No named serving stack version. The prefix-caching and preemption behaviour differs between servers and between releases, and the piece stays general because the specific one he ran is not recorded here.
No incident to open on. The opening is written as a composite; if he has a real ticket with the two contradictory numbers, it replaces the first paragraph and improves it.
excerpt: A streaming endpoint has three latencies and most dashboards graph the wrong one. Five symptoms, the check for each, and the order to fix them in.
